title: Choose the card's direction
question: All four use your navy, gold, logo, Montserrat and Poppins. They differ in how the card is built and what makes it recognisably Gold Aces. Keep the roll, take another card, or re-roll.

options.label: Engraved Certificate
options.thesis: Each staff card carries its own gold guilloche rosette, like a genuine certificate, so the customer knows it is the real Gold Aces contact.
options.viewport: Logo, then a full-width highlight-gold Save Contact; the photo sits in a rosette generated from the staff id; name large, then call, email and website as engraved-ruled rows.
options.risk: If the rosette gets busy it reads old-fashioned or like a price note; it has to stay a hairline frame around the photo.

raised.raise: Phone numbers set in tabular lining figures; hierarchy follows one fixed size ramp.
Everything the customer needs fits one phone screen with no scrolling.
Every engraved rule is drawn at one device pixel, never a thick border.
Hierarchy comes from scale contrast (large name, small labels), not coloured boxes.
Highlight #ffc619 has exactly one job: the Save Contact button.

options.label: The Gold Ace
options.lineage: the ace of spades playing card
options.thesis: The card is an ace: gold-foil corner indices carry the staff member's initials and the spade, like a dealt playing card.
materials: gold foil on lacquered card stock
options.viewport: A tall navy playing card fills the screen; initials and spade in two opposite corners; logo, photo and name centred; Save Contact and the contact rows inside the card face.
options.risk: The literal reading of the brand name, and where most runs for 'Gold Aces' would land; corner indices can tip into gimmick.

options.label: Showroom Wayfinding
options.thesis: Saving the contact is the one decision at the junction, signed in a monumental band of highlight gold.
options.viewport: A highlight-gold band spans the top with Save Contact in large sentence-case type; below, each way to reach the person is its own signed row with a pictogram square and arrow.
options.case: Fuses cleanly and wins on clarity: one decision, signed at scale; loses on audience identification, because buyers think of showrooms, not airports.
options.risk: Can read as transit signage rather than a premium dealership, and the yellow band outweighs the softer brand gold.

options.label: Star Atlas
options.thesis: Contact details plotted like stars on a navy chart.
options.viewport: A navy chart with the name as the brightest star.
options.case: Fuses poorly: car buyers do not identify with star charts, and plotting a phone number obscures it.
options.kept: Tabular figures and a fixed size ramp for hierarchy.

options.label: Mixtape J-card
options.thesis: The contact as a folded inlay card.
options.viewport: A folded inlay with details as a tracklist.
options.case: Fuses poorly: handwritten and casual against a premium dealership.
options.kept: Everything lives on one sheet: the whole card fits one screen.

options.label: Centre-rail Reference
options.thesis: The card set like an annotated reference page.
options.viewport: Two narrow columns around a rail of keys.
options.case: Fuses poorly: a scholarly page for a one-tap task.
options.risk: Too dense for a phone at a dealership.
options.kept: Every rule drawn at one device pixel.

options.label: Type Specimen
options.thesis: The name as a giant specimen glyph.
options.viewport: A giant initial with the details below.
options.case: Fuses poorly: sliders have no job on a contact card.

options.label: Bitmap Specimen
options.viewport: A pixel-type name over fine body text.
options.case: Fuses poorly: lo-fi pixels fight a gold luxury brand.

canonCard.label: Standard digital business card
canonCard.thesis: The familiar contact card, executed cleanly in your colours.
canonCard.viewport: Navy header with logo and Save Contact, round photo, name, then call, email and website as list rows.
canonCard.risk: Indistinguishable from every other e-card service.
